The tactic first | A | B will first try A, then B. If A fails but changes the tactic state, that new state will be visible to B. As a consequence, B may fail even though B would have succeeded in the original state. To put it dfifferently, the order of arguments to first is significant: first | A | B may fail even though first | B | A would succeed.

Is there some variation of first | A | B in which A and B will both run from the original state? In other words, I'd like some way to rewind to the original state if A fails.

To make this concrete, consider:

axiom P : Nat → Prop
axiom Q : Nat → Prop

axiom a : ∀x : Nat, P x → Q x
axiom b : ∀x : Nat, P (x + 1) → Q x

example (x : Nat): P (x + 1) → Q x := by
  intro
  first | apply_rules [a] | apply_rules [b]   -- fails: unsolved goals

The proof above fails, but if I swap the order to

  first | apply_rules [b] | apply_rules [a]

then it succeeds. Is there some way that I can try both apply_rules [a] and apply_rules [b] in a way that will work independent of the order in which I list them?
in this case, apply_rules [a] doesn't close the goal, but it also doesn't fail, so apply_rules [b] is actually never tried

Aha - that works great. Thanks!

I now see that I had misunderstood the situation. I had thought that in first | A | B A could fail but update the tactic state, which would then be handed to B. However, now I see that A may succeed but not close the goal, in which case B doesn't run at all. I wanted to retry B from the beginning if A doesn't completely close the goal. This idiom with done is exactly what I needed - thanks again.

Note that there's another option for similar behavior: first | { A } | { B }, where {} demands the goal is closed. The subtle difference is that done demands that there are no remaining goals at all, whereas {} demands that the main goal you're working on is closed (but allows goals you weren't working on to still be unclosed). So you'd only notice the difference if you had multiple goals before running your tactic. Which one you want depends on whether you want your tactic to close all goals or just the main goal :)
Thomas: This is great to know, thanks!
